sn41.8:0.3: The Jain Ascetic of the Ñātika Clan
sn41.8:1.1: Now at that time the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan had arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa together with a large assembly of Jain ascetics.
sn41.8:1.2: Citta the householder heard that they had arrived.
sn41.8:1.3: Together with several lay followers, he went up to the Jain Ñātika and exchanged greetings with him.
sn41.8:1.4: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Jain Ñātika said to him,
sn41.8:1.5: “Householder, do you have faith in the ascetic Gotama’s claim that
sn41.8:1.6: there is a state of concentration without thinking and considering; that there is the cessation of thinking and considering?”
sn41.8:2.1: “Sir, in this case I don’t rely on faith in the Buddha’s claim that
sn41.8:2.2: there is a state of concentration without thinking and considering; that there is the cessation of thinking and considering.”
sn41.8:2.3: When he said this, the Jain Ñātika looked up at his assembly and said,
sn41.8:2.4: “See, good fellows, how straightforward this householder Citta is! He’s not devious or deceitful at all. To imagine that you can stop thinking and considering would be like imagining that you can catch the wind in a net, or dam the Ganges river with your own hand.”
sn41.8:3.3: “Knowledge is definitely better than faith, householder.”
sn41.8:3.4: “Well sir, whenever I want, fully withdrawn from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I enter and dwell in the first stage of meditation, which has the delight and contentment born of seclusion, with thinking and considering.
sn41.8:3.5: And whenever I want, as thinking and considering are stilled … I enter and dwell in the second stage of meditation.
sn41.8:3.6: And whenever I want, with the fading away of delight … I enter and dwell in the third stage of meditation.
sn41.8:3.7: And whenever I want, giving up pleasure and pain … I enter and dwell in the fourth stage of meditation.
sn41.8:3.8: And so, sir, since I know and see like this, why should I rely on faith in another ascetic or brahmin who claims that
sn41.8:3.9: there is a state of concentration without thinking and considering; that there is the cessation of thinking and considering?”
sn41.8:4.1: When he said this, the Jain Ñātika looked askance at his own assembly and said,
sn41.8:4.2: “See, good fellows, how crooked this householder Citta is! He’s so devious and deceitful!”
sn41.8:5.1: “Sir, just now I understood you to say:
sn41.8:5.2: ‘See, good fellows, how straightforward this householder Citta is! He’s not devious or deceitful at all.’
sn41.8:5.3: But then I understood you to say:
sn41.8:5.4: ‘See, good fellows, how crooked this householder Citta is! He’s so devious and deceitful!’
sn41.8:5.5: If your first statement is true, the second is wrong.
sn41.8:5.6: If your first statement is wrong, the second is true.
sn41.8:5.7: And also, sir, these ten legitimate questions are relevant.
sn41.8:5.8: When you understand what they mean, then, together with your assembly of Jain ascetics, you can rebut me.
sn41.8:5.18: Ten things: question, summary, and answer.’”
sn41.8:5.19: Then Citta got up from his seat and left without asking the Jain Ñātika these ten legitimate questions.
